The table in examples.py is a real local directory tree with real JSON snapshot files and real binary data files, not Iceberg's or Delta's actual on-disk metadata/manifest format — disclosed in the script's own docstring and FACT-CHECK.md red-team #1. What transfers is the real mechanism: snapshot chain, time travel, rollback, expiry, orphan-file removal.

This topic's rollback moves the current pointer directly to an old snapshot's metadata file (Iceberg's own documented behavior), not Delta's RESTORE, which creates a new version — both are real, sourced mechanisms; this topic demonstrates the simpler one and names RESTORE as the equivalent, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #2.

The 'GDPR delete' demo stands in for a real column-level redaction, not an actual row-level DELETE/MERGE statement — the conflict demonstrated (the pre-delete file survives until expiry and vacuum) is the real, sourced conflict regardless of exactly how the delete is expressed in SQL, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #3.

at.step: Reveal: a hard delete isn't gone until vacuum runs — the real GDPR conflict

items.item: The too-short vs. long-enough retention scenarios are simulated by code path (expiry before or after the read completes), not an actual wall-clock race between concurrent processes — a deterministic, sourced reproduction of the documented failure mode, per FACT-CHECK.md red-team #4.

items.item: This topic does not demonstrate Iceberg's separate metadata-file-level cleanup (write.metadata.delete-after-commit) — only snapshot expiry and orphan data-file removal, matching CHAPTER.md's stated scope for this topic.

This topic hosts the §6.3 chapter lab's compaction/expiry/retention leg per CHAPTER.md's own note; the four demonstrations in examples.py already compact, expire, and vacuum a real table and verify time travel fails past the retention window.

Delta's default retention figures (7 days for VACUUM, 30 days for table history) are quoted from the sources but not asserted as literal numbers in examples.py, so they are spoken as words rather than shown as on-screen digits, consistent with the build's digit-provenance check.

The reclaimed-bytes figure shown on screen (40,000 bytes) is the literal FILE_SIZE_BYTES constant from examples.py, traced per-file; the demo's actual total reclaimed across two files (80,000 bytes) is not itself a literal in the source and is therefore not shown as a single on-screen number.
